I don’t have web access in this conversation, so I can only share what I currently recall and infer about Otakar Šín. If you want fully sourced, up-to-date, or more detailed material (works lists, scores, images, citations), I can look it up if you allow me to fetch external information. Here’s what I can tell you now.

Summary
- Otakar Šín was a Czech musician active in the late 19th and first half of the 20th century. He is best known as a music theorist, teacher, and composer.
- He made important contributions to the teaching of harmony and counterpoint in Czechoslovakia, authoring influential textbooks used at conservatories.
- He served as a professor at the Prague Conservatory (and/or other Czech institutions) and influenced generations of Czech composers and musicians through his pedagogy and writings.
- As a theorist, Šín wrote systematic treatments of harmony (including chromatic harmony), form, and counterpoint; his approach was practical and pedagogically oriented, intended for conservatory students.
- He composed, but his theoretical and pedagogical writings are generally considered his principal legacy rather than a large output of widely performed compositions.

Typical topics he covered (in his writings)
- Diatonic and chromatic harmony, including advanced chromaticism and the treatment of altered chords.
- Counterpoint and species counterpoint as a foundation for harmony.
- Form and composition techniques for students.
- Practical exercises and examples drawn from the classical-romantic repertoire and from Czech music.

Historical and cultural context
- Šín worked during a period when Czech musical life was consolidating its national schools (Dvořák, Fibich, Novák, Suk, and others) and when conservatory pedagogy was formalizing. His textbooks helped standardize theoretical instruction in that environment.
- He was part of a broader Central European tradition of thorough, systematized harmony and counterpoint instruction—comparable in purpose to German and French conservatory treatises—even while addressing chromatic tendencies of late Romantic and early 20th-century music.

Legacy and reception
- Within Czech musical education, his textbooks remained in use for many years and influenced teachers and students across the country.
- Outside Czech-speaking areas his name is less widely known; his works have primarily local/historical importance rather than broad international citation like some other theorists.
- Modern scholars and teachers occasionally consult his writings for historical perspective on early-20th-century pedagogy in Central Europe and for practical exercises reflective of that era’s harmonic practices.
